name: Numbers as logical fictions
plain_explanation: Words like 'two' or 'ten' do not name any real thing that percepts contain; when a statement using them is properly spelled out, the number-word disappears, replaced by patterns of 'there is an a... there is a b... a is not b.'
precise_definition: Russell's claim that number-words are 'formal': what verifies 'there are two so-and-sos' is a common logical form shared by many different facts, not a common constituent (unlike, e.g., a proper name that always refers to the same particular thing); properly analysed, a sentence like 'I have two hands' contains no constituent corresponding to the word 'two.'
why_it_mattered: It lets Russell agree with Plato that pure mathematics is not derived from perception (since it consists of tautologies about symbols) while denying that number designates a Platonic Idea perceived by a special faculty of mind.
historical_origin: Developed by Russell in this chapter, drawing on his broader logical analysis of number (referred to elsewhere in his work).
examples: 'I have two hands' analysed as: there is an a and a b, a is not identical with b, and 'x is a hand of mine' is true only when x is a or x is b
The fallacy of arguing 'the earth has one satellite, namely the moon, therefore the moon is one,' compared to 'the Apostles were twelve; Peter was an apostle; therefore Peter was twelve'
competing_positions: Plato's suggestion that 'ten' or 'one,' like 'existence,' names something the mind grasps directly and which is common to sound and colour alike
